facts.fact_text: The applicants listed in the appendix were all professors at Tbilisi State University at the material time.
The applicants held numerous public meetings at Tbilisi State University as part of their activities opposing the reforms.
On 19 June 2006 the already-dissolved Grand Academic Council organised a meeting of Tbilisi State University staff.

After the meeting with Mr G.Kh. ended without results, Tbilisi State University employees — including all of the applicants — decided to stay at the University in one of the lecture halls and hold a further meeting among themselves.
On 20 June 2006 the applicants, along with other employees of Tbilisi State University, gathered again in one of the lecture halls of the University.

On 3 July 2006, in response to a request by the fourth applicant, Mr Sanadze, the acting Rector of Tbilisi State University, Mr G.Kh., authorised a meeting of University employees in the Grand Hall of the main University building between 3.30 p.m. and 7 p.m.
At the meeting of 3 July 2006, the already-dissolved Grand Academic Council 'elected' the second applicant as the new Rector of Tbilisi State University.

After the 'election' of the second applicant as new Rector, a group of about twenty people, including all of the applicants, headed to the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. to inform him of the Grand Academic Council's decision and to demand his resignation.
According to the applicants, they entered acting Rector Mr G.Kh.'s office on 3 July 2006 without using any force and informed him of the Grand Academic Council's decision.
According to the applicants, after the police asked the applicants and others present to leave the acting Rector's office, they left without any resistance and moved to a lecture hall.

According to the case file, after their removal from the acting Rector's office, the applicants together with other protesters — totalling approximately 400 people — gathered in one of the lecture halls of the main Tbilisi State University building and continued their protest.

The two journalists and two professors questioned on 3 August 2006 all claimed that there had been no confrontation — either physical or verbal — in the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. on 3 July 2006.

The two journalists and two professors questioned on 3 August 2006 claimed that the group had been simply demanding the resignation of Mr G.Kh. and that they had left the office at the request of the police.
According to the applicants, at around 1 a.m. on 20 June 2006 the police arrived at Tbilisi State University.
According to the applicants, the police forced everyone out of the Tbilisi State University building without giving any explanations or prior warning.
Towards the evening of 20 June 2006 the police allegedly again dispersed the applicants' meeting at Tbilisi State University.
While the meeting at acting Rector Mr G.Kh.'s office continued, the police entered the Tbilisi State University grounds.
The police officers went directly to the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh., who immediately left the room upon their arrival.
According to the applicants, after the police asked the applicants and others present to leave the acting Rector's office, they left without any resistance and moved to a lecture hall.

According to the case file, after their removal from the acting Rector's office, the applicants together with other protesters — totalling approximately 400 people — gathered in one of the lecture halls of the main Tbilisi State University building and continued their protest.
The applicants alleged that at around 11 p.m. on 3 July 2006 the police closed the doors of the lecture hall and prevented the people inside from leaving.
The applicants alleged that they had been locked in the lecture hall without access to water, food or toilet facilities until approximately 8-10 a.m. on 4 July 2006.

By a decision of 4 August 2006, the Tbilisi City Court found the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth applicants guilty of administrative offences under Articles 166, 173 and 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Tbilisi City Court imposed a fine of 100 Georgian laris (approximately 45 euros) on each of the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth applicants.

The Tbilisi City Court found the sixth applicant, Ms Sikharulidze, and the ninth applicant, Mr D. Bakhtadze, guilty of administrative offences under Articles 166 and 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences only, imposing a fine of 100 Georgian laris on each of them.
On 4 September 2006, the chairwoman of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, sitting privately and without holding an oral hearing, dismissed the applicants' appeal as unsubstantiated.

Article 1(1) of the Law of Georgia on Assembly and Demonstrations, as worded at the material time, provided that the law regulates the exercise of the right guaranteed by the Constitution of Georgia to gather publicly, unarmed, both indoors and outdoors, without prior permission.

Article 9(1) of the Law of Georgia on Assembly and Demonstrations, as worded at the material time, prohibited holding an assembly or a demonstration inside the building of the Parliament of Georgia, the residency of the President of Georgia, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Georgia, on the premises of courts, prosecutor's offices or of police, penitentiary or military units and sites, in railway stations, airports, hospitals or diplomatic missions (or within a 20-metre radius thereof), on the premises of governmental institutions or local self-government bodies, or in the buildings of companies, institutions and organisations that operate under special labour security rules or are under armed guard.
The Code of Administrative Offences of Georgia was adopted on 15 December 1984, when Georgia was part of the Soviet Union, and subsequently numerous amendments were introduced.

Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences of Georgia, as in force at the material time, defined minor hooliganism (a minor breach of public order) as swearing and cursing in a public place, causing insulting harassment to a person, or other similar actions which disturb public order and peace, punishable by a fine of 100 Georgian laris or, if that measure was not deemed sufficient, up to thirty days' administrative detention.

Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences of Georgia, as in force at the material time, provided that maliciously disobeying a lawful instruction or order issued by a law enforcement officer shall be punishable by a fine amounting to ten times the minimum monthly wage, or by one to six months' correctional labour compounded by the withholding of 20% of the offender's wages, or, if those measures were not deemed sufficient, by up to thirty days' administrative detention.

Article 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences of Georgia, as in force at the material time, defined arbitrary behaviour as the exercise of a right in violation of a law which does not cause any significant damage to people, the State or to public bodies, punishable by a warning or a fine of half the minimum monthly wage, or in the case of public officials, a warning or a fine of one minimum monthly wage.

In reaching its decision, the Tbilisi City Court concluded that the Grand Academic Council had begun acting unlawfully from 8 June 2005, when the old Tbilisi State University charter had been repealed by Presidential Decree no. 473.
The Tbilisi City Court found that the restoration of the dissolved Grand Academic Council and the election of the new University Rector on 3 July 2006 had been unlawful.

The Tbilisi City Court dismissed the applicants' argument that the acting Rector's office was merely a private working space, reasoning that the presence of the public rendered it a public space for the purposes of the Code of Administrative Offences.

In their appeal, the applicants complained that there had been no record of an administrative offence having been made individually in respect of each of them and that their individual roles in the commission of the impugned administrative offences had not been established.
In their appeal, the applicants complained that the proceedings had been brought in a manner suggesting their collective liability.

In their appeal, the applicants referred to witness statements noting that there had been two hundred people outside and twenty people inside the acting Rector's office during the events of 3 July 2006 and that it was impossible to identify the individuals who had allegedly insulted the acting Rector and forced their way into his office.

The Tbilisi City Court found that the subsequent demand for the resignation of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. in view of the election had been unlawful and constituted the administrative offence of arbitrary behaviour within the meaning of Article 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the applicants' behaviour had amounted to insulting harassment with respect to Mr G.Kh. and other staff present, and to 'other similar action' that had violated public order and peace.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that although persons are entitled to exercise the rights and freedoms enshrined in Articles 19, 24 and 25 of the Constitution of Georgia, they are obliged in the process of exercising those rights to abstain from violating others' rights and interests, from encroaching upon others' honour and dignity, and from violating public order.

Article 24(4) of the Constitution of Georgia provides that the exercise of the rights listed in Article 24(1) and (2) may be subject only to such limitations as are prescribed by law and are necessary in a democratic society in the interests of state security, territorial integrity or public safety, to prevent crime, to safeguard rights and dignity of others, to prevent disclosure of information acknowledged as confidential, or to ensure the independence and impartiality of justice.
According to the applicants, the police forced everyone out of the Tbilisi State University building without giving any explanations or prior warning.
According to the applicants, despite the applicants' repeated requests, the police officers did not show them any order authorising the removal of the people gathered at Tbilisi State University.
According to the applicants, they entered acting Rector Mr G.Kh.'s office on 3 July 2006 without using any force and informed him of the Grand Academic Council's decision.
According to the applicants, after the police asked the applicants and others present to leave the acting Rector's office, they left without any resistance and moved to a lecture hall.
The applicants alleged that at around 11 p.m. on 3 July 2006 the police closed the doors of the lecture hall and prevented the people inside from leaving.
The applicants alleged that they had been locked in the lecture hall without access to water, food or toilet facilities until approximately 8-10 a.m. on 4 July 2006.
According to the applicants, on 4 July 2006 the Minister of Education of Georgia held a press briefing denouncing the events that had taken place at Tbilisi State University on 3 July 2006.
According to the applicants, at the press briefing on 4 July 2006 the Minister of Education referred to those involved in the 3 July 2006 events as 'hooligans'.

According to the applicants, at the press briefing on 4 July 2006 the Minister of Education gave an assurance that all those involved in the 3 July 2006 events would bear responsibility for their actions.

In the letter of 24 July 2006 to the President of Georgia, the applicants made a particular complaint that they, along with several hundred other people, had been locked in the Tbilisi State University lecture hall for the whole night of 3-4 July 2006.

In the letter of 24 July 2006 to the President of Georgia, the applicants alleged that being locked in the lecture hall had amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, as they had been denied access to drinking water and a toilet and had been left without fresh air.
The prosecutor's ruling of 29 July 2006 did not mention the applicants' complaint concerning the events of 19-20 June 2006.

At the hearing of 30 July 2006, the applicants objected that owing to the initiation of the administrative proceedings they could not avail themselves of the opportunity to challenge the prosecutorial ruling of 29 July 2006.
At the hearing of 30 July 2006, the applicants complained that they had not had sufficient time to acquaint themselves with the relevant material in the case file and to hire a lawyer.

At the hearing on 3 August 2006, the judge refused the applicants' request for the questioning of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. and his deputy, reasoning that those two individuals had already been questioned at the pre-trial stage and that their statements had been included in the case file.

At the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants tried to put several questions to the prosecutor regarding the alleged locking in the lecture hall, but the presiding judge dismissed the questions as irrelevant and having no bearing on the case.

At the hearing of 3 August 2006, police patrol officer G.Ch. clarified in reply to a question that no one had physically resisted the police, but that the protesters had simply refused to leave the acting Rector's office.

At the hearing of 3 August 2006, the third police officer, K.B., similarly maintained that there had been no physical confrontation inside the acting Rector's office, but that it had taken a while before those inside had agreed to leave.

The two journalists and two professors questioned on 3 August 2006 all claimed that there had been no confrontation — either physical or verbal — in the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. on 3 July 2006.

The two journalists and two professors questioned on 3 August 2006 claimed that the group had been simply demanding the resignation of Mr G.Kh. and that they had left the office at the request of the police.

By a decision of 4 August 2006, the Tbilisi City Court found the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth applicants guilty of administrative offences under Articles 166, 173 and 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Tbilisi City Court imposed a fine of 100 Georgian laris (approximately 45 euros) on each of the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth applicants.

The Tbilisi City Court found the sixth applicant, Ms Sikharulidze, and the ninth applicant, Mr D. Bakhtadze, guilty of administrative offences under Articles 166 and 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences only, imposing a fine of 100 Georgian laris on each of them.

In their appeal, the applicants complained that there had been no record of an administrative offence having been made individually in respect of each of them and that their individual roles in the commission of the impugned administrative offences had not been established.
In their appeal, the applicants complained that the proceedings had been brought in a manner suggesting their collective liability.

In their appeal, the applicants referred to witness statements noting that there had been two hundred people outside and twenty people inside the acting Rector's office during the events of 3 July 2006 and that it was impossible to identify the individuals who had allegedly insulted the acting Rector and forced their way into his office.
In their appeal, the applicants complained of the failure of the Tbilisi City Court to examine acting Rector Mr G.Kh. and his deputy in the course of the trial.

In their appeal, the applicants challenged the categorisation of their actions as administrative offences by the Tbilisi City Court, submitting that they had simply been exercising their freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.
On 4 September 2006, the chairwoman of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, sitting privately and without holding an oral hearing, dismissed the applicants' appeal as unsubstantiated.
The operative part of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal's decision of 4 September 2006 indicated that no further appeal was possible.
